title: Nasogastric Tube Feeding
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Feeding and Elimination Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Indications for Nasogastric Tube Feeding
headings.content: Nasogastric (NG) tube feeding is a vital clinical intervention utilized in Nigerian healthcare settings when patients are unable to meet their nutritional requirements orally due to physical, neurological, or psychological limitations. The primary indication for an NG tube is short-term enteral nutrition, typically defined as expected use for less than four to six weeks. Clinical scenarios necessitating NG tube placement include severe dysphagia following a cerebrovascular accident (stroke), facial or upper gastrointestinal trauma, severe protein-energy malnutrition where the gut is functional, head and neck malignancies, and impaired level of consciousness where airway protection and nutrition are compromised. It is also frequently indicated for gastric decompression to relieve nausea, vomiting, or abdominal distension associated with bowel obstruction or ileus, as well as for administering medications to patients unable to swallow safely. Contraindications must be carefully evaluated prior to insertion and include severe midface trauma, basilar skull fractures, esophageal strictures or atresia, and recent esophageal or gastric surgery. As nursing students preparing for clinical practice in Nigeria, recognizing these indications and contraindications ensures safe, effective, and patient-centered care, preventing life-threatening complications such as intracranial tube misplacement or esophageal perforation. Understanding the clinical context helps nurses educate patients and families, easing anxiety and promoting compliance with nutritional therapy regimens.

headings.title: Pre-Procedure Assessment and Patient Preparation
headings.content: Pre-procedure assessment and patient preparation are critical nursing responsibilities that lay the foundation for a safe nasogastric tube insertion. Before beginning the procedure, the nurse must review the medical record for any contraindications, verify the physician's order, and perform a comprehensive physical assessment of the patient. This includes assessing the patency of both nares, inspecting the nasal mucosa for inflammation, polyps, or previous trauma, evaluating bowel sounds, and assessing the patient's abdominal distension and neurological status. Obtaining informed consent is essential; the nurse must explain the procedure clearly to the conscious patient or their caregiver, addressing fears and explaining sensations such as gagging or discomfort during insertion. Establishing a reliable communication system, such as a hand signal, allows the patient to indicate the need to pause the procedure. Positioning the patient properly is another key preparatory step: the conscious patient should be placed in a high Fowler's position (90 degrees) to facilitate swallowing and reduce the risk of aspiration, while the unconscious patient should be positioned appropriately with the head elevated if permitted. Measuring the correct insertion length is calculated by measuring from the tip of the nose to the earlobe, and then down to the xiphoid process (NEX measurement), marking the length with tape or noting a specific measurement on the tube. Thorough preparation minimizes anxiety, enhances cooperation, and reduces procedural risks.

headings.title: Equipment Needed for Nasogastric Tube Insertion and Feeding
headings.content: Gathering the correct equipment before initiating nasogastric tube insertion and feeding ensures efficiency, patient safety, and adherence to aseptic or clean technique standards. Essential items for insertion include the appropriate size and type of NG tube—such as Levin or Ryles tubes for feeding and decompression, or smaller bore polyurethane feeding tubes. Other mandatory insertion supplies are a clean pair of gloves, water-soluble lubricating jelly to ease passage and reduce mucosal trauma, a 50 mL or larger catheter-tip syringe for aspiration and verification, a stethoscope to auscultate air insufflation, hypoallergenic adhesive tape or securing device to anchor the tube, a tongue depressor and penlight to inspect the oral cavity, a glass of water with a straw (if the patient can swallow), and a basin or emesis bag for comfort. For the subsequent feeding phase, necessary equipment includes the prescribed enteral formula at room temperature, a feeding bag or syringe depending on the delivery method (bolus or continuous), and sterile or clean water for flushes before and after feeding and medication administration. Personal protective equipment such as masks and eye protection should also be available according to institutional infection control policies. Having all supplies organized at the bedside prevents interruptions during the procedure, thereby minimizing patient distress and the risk of complications.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Nasogastric Tube Insertion
headings.content: The step-by-step procedure for nasogastric tube insertion requires precision, patience, and effective communication between the nurse and the patient. After performing hand hygiene and donning clean gloves, the nurse selects the more patent naris by asking the patient to occlude each nostril and breathe. The calculated NEX length is marked on the tube with tape or noted. The tip of the tube is lubricated with a water-soluble lubricant for about 10 to 20 cm. The nurse instructs the patient to hyperextend the neck slightly as the tube is gently inserted through the nostril, aiming downward and backward toward the ear. Once the tube reaches the nasopharynx and the patient feels it in the throat, the nurse instructs the patient to flex the head forward toward the chest and begin swallowing sips of water (if permitted) or dry swallowing. Swallowing closes the trachea and opens the esophagus, facilitating smooth advancement of the tube to the pre-determined mark. If the patient exhibits coughing, choking, cyanosis, or significant drop in oxygen saturation, the nurse must immediately stop and withdraw the tube, as these are signs of respiratory tract placement. Once the target mark is reached, the tube is temporarily anchored to the nose using tape to prevent dislodgement before placement is definitively verified. Documenting patient tolerance throughout the procedure is essential.

headings.title: Methods for Verifying Nasogastric Tube Placement
headings.content: Verifying the correct placement of a nasogastric tube before initiating any feeding, medication administration, or fluid instillation is a critical nursing competency that prevents fatal complications such as pulmonary aspiration of nutritional formulas. The gold standard for confirming placement is radiographic verification (X-ray), which should always be performed after initial insertion and before the first feeding. However, nurses must also utilize bedside verification methods for ongoing checks prior to each intermittent feeding or medication administration. These methods include measuring the external tube length and comparing it against the documented insertion measurement, observing the appearance of aspirated fluid, and testing the pH of gastric aspirate. Gastric fluid is typically acidic, with a pH ranging from 1 to 4 (or up to 5.5 if the patient is receiving acid-inhibiting medications), whereas respiratory secretions are generally alkaline (pH 7.0 or higher), and intestinal fluid usually has a pH of 6.0 or higher. Visual assessment of aspirate can also guide the nurse: gastric fluid is often grassy green, tan, off-white, or bloody, whereas respiratory fluid is typically clear or tinged with mucus. Historic bedside methods such as auscultating air insufflation (listening over the epigastrium while injecting air) are unreliable and no longer recommended by safety organizations as a sole indicator because sounds can be transmitted from the respiratory tract or bowel. Ensuring accurate verification protects patient safety in every clinical shift.

headings.title: Administering Enteral Feedings and Water Flushes
headings.content: Administering enteral feedings and water flushes requires strict adherence to aseptic technique, proper positioning, and regular monitoring to ensure patient comfort and prevent complications like aspiration and tube occlusion. Before initiating any feeding, the nurse must verify tube placement and assess gastric residual volume (GRV) if required by institutional policy, returning the residual unless it exceeds specified parameters (commonly 200–250 mL or more). The patient must be positioned with the head of the bed elevated at least 30 to 45 degrees, a position that should be maintained during the feeding and for at least 30 to 60 minutes afterward to prevent aspiration. Feedings can be administered via intermittent bolus using a syringe, intermittent gravity drip, or continuous infusion using an electronic pump. The nurse must ensure the formula is at room temperature and check the expiration date. Water flushes are an essential component of tube maintenance: the nurse should flush the tube with 30 mL of sterile or clean water before and after each intermittent feeding, after medication administration, and every 4 to 6 hours during continuous feedings to prevent clogging. Medications must be thoroughly crushed (if formulation permits) and dissolved in warm water, administered separately, and never mixed directly into the enteral formula. Documenting the total fluid intake, formula type, and volume administered ensures accurate fluid balance tracking for Nigerian nursing students and healthcare teams.

headings.title: Monitoring, Maintenance, and Prevention of Complications
headings.content: Monitoring, maintenance, and the prevention of complications are continuous nursing responsibilities throughout the duration of nasogastric tube therapy. Nurses must routinely inspect the nasal mucosa and skin around the nares for pressure ulcers, necrosis, or irritation caused by tape friction, changing the securing tape and repositioning the tube as needed per hospital protocol. Oral and nasal hygiene is vital; providing frequent mouth care, lubricating lips, and offering throat lozenges or ice chips (if allowed) relieve dryness and discomfort. To prevent tube occlusion, meticulous flushing protocols must be followed, and blocked tubes should be managed promptly using warm water flushes or prescribed enzyme solutions under clinical guidelines. Gastrointestinal complications such as diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and constipation must be monitored closely and reported, as they may indicate rapid infusion rates, formula intolerance, or bacterial contamination. Pulmonary aspiration remains the most dangerous complication; nurses must ensure head-of-bed elevation is maintained and immediately stop feedings if the patient exhibits coughing, shortness of breath, or unexplained respiratory distress. Metabolic complications, including hyperglycemia and electrolyte imbalances, require regular laboratory monitoring. Diligent nursing care safeguards the patient's recovery and overall well-being.

headings.title: Documentation and Nasogastric Tube Removal
headings.content: Documentation and the safe removal of a nasogastric tube mark the final phases of enteral tube therapy. Comprehensive nursing documentation is legally and clinically required; the nurse must record the date and time of insertion, tube size and type, naris used, verification method results (e.g., pH and X-ray findings), patient tolerance, and the amount and type of initial drainage or feed administered. During ongoing care, accurate records of all fluid intakes, residual volumes, tube flushes, and skin condition must be maintained. When the patient is able to resume adequate oral nutrition or if the tube is no longer clinically indicated, the physician orders its removal. To remove an NG tube, the nurse explains the procedure to the patient, performs hand hygiene, dons gloves, and places a towel or waterproof pad across the patient's chest. The tube is disconnected from suction or feeding equipment, and any tape securing the tube to the nose is gently removed. The nurse instructs the patient to take a deep breath and hold it (which closes the glottis and prevents aspiration), and then smoothly, steadily, and rapidly withdraws the tube. The tube is immediately placed in a disposal bag, and oral hygiene is provided to restore patient comfort. Finally, the nurse documents the time of removal, the integrity of the removed tube (ensuring the tip is intact), the patient's tolerance, and the patient's post-removal respiratory and abdominal status.
